source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3

coverage.scope: C. trustee four options, court approval and timing; D. standards and legal consequences of rejection; Enron full case on date of calculating rejection damages; 8.2(a,b),8.3 unsolved

topics.title: C.1 Four Options: Assume, Assume–Assign, Reject, Do Nothing
topics.description: The bankruptcy estate's contractual choice and marginal value analysis.

entries.title: Assumption §365(a): full estate obligations with court approval
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: Assumption binds estate to executory contract's benefits and burdens, obligates contract performance and may grant counterparty administrative treatment; may be worthwhile if gain from counterparty exceeds performance cost.
entries.laymanExplanation: Estate accepts both discounted delivery price and its own promised $5k payment.
entries.legalExplanation: Court approval §365(a) and defaults cure under §365(b) are distinct prerequisites.
entries.examApplication: Compare market value with contract price and other cost, not merely presence of contract.
entries.examTrap: Assumption is not automatic because trustee used goods in limbo.

entries.title: Assume and assign §365(f): monetize favorable deal
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: Trustee may assume contract and assign it for consideration to third party subject statutory restrictions; §365(k) generally releases estate from postassignment breach liability.
entries.laymanExplanation: Lease at below-market rent can be sold to a new store for profit.
entries.legalExplanation: Must first assume and cure, and assignee must provide adequate assurance, even without existing default.
entries.examApplication: Calculate value of remaining contract surplus, consider cure and sale fees.
entries.examTrap: Cannot skip assumption step and assign raw burdens.

entries.title: Rejection = refuse estate burden, §365(g) prefiling breach
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: Rejection avoids taking over contract performance and generally leaves nondebtor with prepetition general unsecured damage claim; estate loses ability to compel ordinary contract benefits.
entries.laymanExplanation: Bad $5k inventory deal can be declined, supplier gets bankruptcy claim rather than full payment.
entries.legalExplanation: After Chapter11 rejection contract can have surviving previously granted property rights despite estate ceasing performance.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish rejection's claim effect from contract termination/rescission.
entries.examTrap: Rejecting contract is not erasing all third-party rights.

entries.title: Do nothing: nondebtor remains bound during limbo
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: Pending choice, counterparty must continue performing; estate can receive postpetition benefits without formal assumption, subject payment for actual benefit as administrative cost; nondebtor may ask court for deadline.
entries.laymanExplanation: Debtor asks vendor to keep delivering while deciding whether to sign on long term.
entries.legalExplanation: Bildisco, Whitcomb address one-way interim enforcement; special lease rules deviate.
entries.examApplication: Check whether §365(d) deadline or special landlord provisions apply.
entries.examTrap: Limbo is not automatically free service nor implied assumption.

entries.title: Economic choice includes opportunity costs and claim distributions
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: Trustee evaluates whether advantageous deal increases estate value given price, market alternative, future revenue and pro rata unsecured distribution if rejected; never simply ignore breach claim.
entries.laymanExplanation: A $5k buy contract may be cheap or expensive depending on market; rejection claim payout matters.
entries.legalExplanation: Book's Problem8.2 varies market to $6k vs $4k and 10% unsecured recoveries.
entries.examApplication: Set separate cash-flows for assumption versus rejection and other alternatives.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume reduced unsecured payout itself makes rejection legal on all facts.

topics.title: C.2–3 Court Approval and Chapter-/Lease-Specific Deadlines
topics.description: Formal court order and distinct Chapter7/Chapter11/nonresidential lease clocks.

entries.title: Formal approval for assumption, rejection and prerequisite assignment
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: §365(a) requires court approval for estate's affirmative assumption/rejection; §365(f)(2)(A) links assignment to assumption. 'Implied' assumption merely from continued performance rejected by source courts.
entries.laymanExplanation: Using seller's services in bankruptcy isn't signing entire contract on the estate's behalf.
entries.legalExplanation: Special deemed rejections can occur AUTOMATICALLY without a separate rejection order.
entries.examApplication: Look for express order, passive statutory expiration or merely services received.
entries.examTrap: Do not infer assumption from business operation under contract.

entries.title: Chapter7 §365(d)(1) 60-day default deadline
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: In Chapter7 trustee must assume or reject executory contract/ordinary unexpired lease within 60 days or obtain extension in time; otherwise deemed rejected. Special nonresidential real-property lease rule §365(d)(4) controls those leases.
entries.laymanExplanation: Chapter7 trustee generally has only two months to commit.
entries.legalExplanation: §365(d)(1) applies presumptively to ordinary contracts except special lease regime.
entries.examApplication: Calculate from order for relief/petition as source says with any extension.
entries.examTrap: Do not apply Chapter11 until-confirmation default to Chapter7.

entries.title: Reorganization §§365(d)(2) until plan confirmation (unless special lease)
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: Chapter9/11/12/13 trustee/DIP may choose up to confirmation, but other party can move for court-set earlier reasonable deadline; balances estate ability to evaluate versus nondebtor's uncertainty.
entries.laymanExplanation: Supplier might compel earlier yes/no if indefinite limbo harms its business.
entries.legalExplanation: Business judgment by DIP to defer; court's power shorten timing.
entries.examApplication: Mention confirmed plan date and creditor motion to expedite.
entries.examTrap: No unlimited limbo if §365(d)(4) applies.

entries.title: Nonresidential property §365(d)(4): 120 days + one 90-day extension
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: In any chapter, commercial realty lease ordinarily must be assumed/rejected within 120 days after order for relief or at earlier plan confirmation; court may allow one 90-day extension for cause, further extension only with lessor prior WRITTEN consent; otherwise deemed rejected.
entries.laymanExplanation: Retail store has about 4 months plus perhaps 3 more, not endless Chapter11 option.
entries.legalExplanation: 2005 change tightened previous open-ended extensions, important to retailers.
entries.examApplication: Construct deadline and determine if landlord consent exists for more time.
entries.examTrap: Do not substitute personal property §365(d)(5) 60-day performance clock.

entries.title: Timing protects nondebtor counterparty's planning
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: Lender/lessor/provider wants prompt cure, assurance or freedom to replace customer; trustee prefers time to see whether deal profitable, but assumption after delay may impose costly admin exposure.
entries.laymanExplanation: Supplier cannot commit capacity to another customer while estate undecided.
entries.legalExplanation: Judge can compel earlier decision where burden to counterparty outweighs estate information needs.
entries.examApplication: Explain timing as litigation leverage and effects of early/later motion.
entries.examTrap: Court does not always favor debtor regardless hardship.

topics.title: D.1 Standard for Rejection: Business Judgment Versus Special CBA Rule
topics.description: Even profitable contracts may be rejected to produce greater estate value.

entries.title: Business judgment standard: defer unless bad faith/gross abuse
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: For ordinary executory contracts, majority permits rejection if it advances estate's interests, even where contract not losing money; court usually defers to trustee absent bad faith or gross misuse of discretion.
entries.laymanExplanation: Company can break a reasonably profitable deal if another better one increases estate benefit after claims.
entries.legalExplanation: Contrast small minority requiring negative/burdensome net value and cases balancing grave counterparty harm.
entries.examApplication: Assess projected economic gain, not automatic rejection because creditors pay pennies.
entries.examTrap: General §365(a) business judgment differs from §1113 CBA balance-of-equities.

entries.title: Rejection need not mean contract is net burdensome
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: Many courts allow rejection of a profitable contract where debtor can earn more elsewhere, because resulting unsecured damages may receive small dividend; source cites railroad precedent and In re Minges.
entries.laymanExplanation: A $5.5k resale on $5k purchase can still be outperformed via other supplier despite positive contract profit.
entries.legalExplanation: This creates externalization of rejection losses to counterparty and other unsecured claimants.
entries.examApplication: Problem8.3 tests profitable original deal and other party's potential financial ruin.
entries.examTrap: Don't automatically deny rejection solely because contract price lower than resale price.

entries.title: Minority approaches: real burden or third-party hardship
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: Some courts require that performance actually lose money; others balance harm to nondebtor if disproportionately worse than benefit to estate, but predominant rule focuses estate's benefit.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some judges would not permit marginal estate saving to bankrupt innocent seller.
entries.legalExplanation: Exception for CBA expressly changes standard through §1113.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish alternate doctrinal tests when prompt asks fairness.
entries.examTrap: Minority approach is not majority holding.

entries.title: Mistaken belief in rejection effects may defeat sound business judgment
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: Trustee who thinks rejection cancels prior property grants or unilaterally strips license may wrongly calculate expected value; if expected benefit legally unavailable, business judgment flawed.
entries.laymanExplanation: Decision isn't rational when estimated gain depends on power trustee doesn't have.
entries.legalExplanation: Mission Product corrects rescission misunderstanding; Ortiz equitable claim question.
entries.examApplication: Before evaluating rejection value identify rights surviving breach.
entries.examTrap: Rejection isn't §544–553 avoidance.

topics.title: D.2 Two Core Principles and Four Effects of Rejection
topics.description: Not assumption; rejection deemed breach, priority and discharge.

entries.title: Principle 1: rejection is NOT assumption
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: Estate neither undertakes future duties nor can require future contract benefits under ongoing performance; prebankruptcy contract remains subject to ordinary nonbankruptcy breach consequences.
entries.laymanExplanation: Trustee says no to paying future $5k and ordinarily cannot force Jones to deliver gizmos.
entries.legalExplanation: Don't treat rejection as contract rescission, cancellation, completed termination or avoidance of property conveyance.
entries.examApplication: Break down estate obligations vs debtor rights separately.
entries.examTrap: Estate avoiding duty doesn't remove every independent state-law injunction or existing license right.

entries.title: Principle 2: rejection constitutes a BREACH §365(g)
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: Rejection itself produces breach, typically deemed immediately prepetition under §365(g)(1), even if contract fully current at filing—anticipatory repudiation.
entries.laymanExplanation: If company rejects otherwise good future delivery deal, seller becomes breached party.
entries.legalExplanation: Prepetition fiction determines priority and interacts with §502(g)(1); disputed extent for damage measuring addressed in Enron.
entries.examApplication: Use actual date of motion vs deemed petition date distinctly.
entries.examTrap: Don't conflate statutory deemed breach with literal physical termination of contract.

entries.title: Four consequences of rejection
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: (1) Estate not liable for future contractual performance; (2) estate not entitled to future counterparty performance; (3) counterparty has a prepetition-classified unsecured claim §502(g)(1); (4) claim-as-debt may be discharged to extent monetary rights qualify under §§101(5),(12).
entries.laymanExplanation: Estate drops the deal and seller generally gets ordinary pennies-on-dollar damage claim, not full administrative payoff.
entries.legalExplanation: Surviving nonmonetary rights require separate §101(5)(B) analysis and nonbankruptcy remedies.
entries.examApplication: In fact-pattern enumerate each with caveat previously conveyed license/property interests.
entries.examTrap: Not every right to injunction is dischargeable money claim.

entries.title: Assumed and later rejected is different (§365(g)(2))
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: If estate first assumes, its subsequent breach/rejection is treated as postpetition obligation and may yield administrative damages, subject later special §503(b)(7) cap for assumed nonresidential real estate lease.
entries.laymanExplanation: A promise newly adopted by estate can be much more expensive to break.
entries.legalExplanation: Klein Sleep source illustrates pre-2005 rule then explicitly discusses 2005 override.
entries.examApplication: Always ask WAS contract formally assumed before rejection.
entries.examTrap: Don't classify assumed-then-rejected damages as ordinary prepetition by reflex.

entries.title: Rejection does NOT rescind prior grants
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: Prepetition property/license rights already transferred survive absent applicable nonbankruptcy termination upon ordinary breach; bankruptcy estate cannot recapture more than debtor owned §541.
entries.laymanExplanation: Trademark license granted years before is not revoked merely by debtor's rejection.
entries.legalExplanation: Mission Product clarified rejecting licensor can't destroy licensee rights, except generally applicable law effects.
entries.examApplication: Identify preexisting property interests separately from promise of future services.
entries.examTrap: Do not treat rejection as undoing conveyance or avoidance.

topics.title: D.2 In re Enron (2005) — Full Rejection-Damages Valuation Case
topics.description: Deemed petition-day breach versus actual rejection-day market price.

entries.title: In re Enron Corp., 330 B.R. 387 (Bankr. S.D.N.Y. 2005)
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: Court accepted deemed PREPETITION valuation date and sustained debtor objection to Taunton's claim, rather than $6.66m actual-rejection calculation. Court reasoned §502(g)(1) says claims 'determined' AND 'allowed' as if prepetition, and treated 'determined' as setting boundaries/amount as of petition date.
entries.laymanExplanation: Under Enron bankruptcy court's statutory construction, calculate rejection damages as of deemed prepetition breach, not actual later rejection; notwithstanding real economic change during limbo.
entries.legalExplanation: Court followed American HomePatient reading both 'determined' and 'allowed' so not surplusage; federal Code controls timing absent gap for state contract remedy. Distinguished Lavigne's nontermination/option timeline because statute didn't fix option deadline there. Petition-date settlement fiction administratively efficient and equitable among creditors. Taunton argued UCC losses only real on actual breach and it could not avoid overpriced purchases while waiting; court responded nondebtor could ask court to compel earlier §365(d)(2) choice. Casebook critiques formal fiction used to deny actual loss and contrasts Chicago Auditorium history/possible alternative reading 'determine' as classify.
entries.examApplication: Contrast $6,658,885 actual-date claimed loss to $0 deemed-date court allowed, $3.28m contract-in-Enron-favor at petition; illustrate $567k interim above-market payments.
entries.examTrap: This is Enron court's holding, not necessarily a universal uncontroversial rule in all jurisdictions or a holding that rejection actually terminated contract.
entries.sourceRole: Full judicial opinion excerpted in uploaded Chapter8
entries.facts: Enron Power Marketing agreed November2 2001 to supply electricity to Taunton municipal utility Jan2002–Dec2007. Enron bankruptcy commenced Dec2 2001. Under contract postpetition Taunton paid $567,216 MORE in 2002 than lower market alternative. By Dec2002 market rose above contract price; EPMI rejected effective December17, deliveries ceased after Dec31. Taunton calculated replacement purchase premium $6,594,885 + $64k costs = $6,658,885 rejection claim using actual rejection value. Debtor said on Nov30 2001 market position favored Enron ~$3.28m, so Taunton loss $0 at deemed breach date. Court had to select valuation date.
entries.issue: Under §§365(g)(1),502(g)(1), is rejection damage claim measured using prepetition DEEMED breach market conditions or actual postpetition REJECTION date for continuing power supply contract?
entries.holding: Court accepted deemed PREPETITION valuation date and sustained debtor objection to Taunton's claim, rather than $6.66m actual-rejection calculation. Court reasoned §502(g)(1) says claims 'determined' AND 'allowed' as if prepetition, and treated 'determined' as setting boundaries/amount as of petition date.
entries.reasoning: Court followed American HomePatient reading both 'determined' and 'allowed' so not surplusage; federal Code controls timing absent gap for state contract remedy. Distinguished Lavigne's nontermination/option timeline because statute didn't fix option deadline there. Petition-date settlement fiction administratively efficient and equitable among creditors. Taunton argued UCC losses only real on actual breach and it could not avoid overpriced purchases while waiting; court responded nondebtor could ask court to compel earlier §365(d)(2) choice. Casebook critiques formal fiction used to deny actual loss and contrasts Chicago Auditorium history/possible alternative reading 'determine' as classify.
entries.rule: Under Enron bankruptcy court's statutory construction, calculate rejection damages as of deemed prepetition breach, not actual later rejection; notwithstanding real economic change during limbo.

entries.title: §502(g)(1) 'determined' versus 'allowed' controversy
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: Enron court reads 'determined' to set amount/time and 'allowed' to assign claim status, so values as prepetition. Book offers competing interpretation 'determined' might classify type, leaving nonbankruptcy actual-breach damages.
entries.laymanExplanation: Why date matters: market moved from seller advantage to buyer advantage during year.
entries.legalExplanation: This is one of professor's statutory construction comparison questions.
entries.examApplication: Give court holding and criticism separately, never silently choose normative interpretation.
entries.examTrap: Textbook questions are not court holdings.

entries.title: Rejection breach legal fiction versus nontermination
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: Enron distinguished Lavigne: rejection is prefiling deemed breach for claim fixing, but contract's actual continued performance and some option expiration rights may remain effective until real postfiling events.
entries.laymanExplanation: Legal fiction affects specific Code classification even while people actually traded power for months.
entries.legalExplanation: Contrast separate question of what claims survive with date for damage measurement under Enron.
entries.examApplication: Use statute purpose and nonbankruptcy contract rules in counterargument.
entries.examTrap: Do not say debtor literally ceased all obligations on bankruptcy petition date.

entries.title: Nondebtor may seek expedited decision under §365(d)(2)
entries.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
entries.summary: Court suggested Taunton could petition for order requiring earlier assume/reject to reduce limbo harm, but book questions whether this is realistic/reasonable substitute for actual market losses.
entries.laymanExplanation: A utility that must keep buying power could ask judge to force earlier decision.
entries.legalExplanation: Decision timing is a procedural safeguard, not affirmative compensation remedy.
entries.examApplication: In answer explain limits of counterparty's bargaining position.
entries.examTrap: Potential expedited motion is not guarantee court grants it.

topics.title: C–D Problems 8.2(a,b), 8.3: Economic Choice and Third-Party Harm (Unsolved)
topics.description: Original gizmo values, unsecured dividends, profitability and harm.

problems.title: Problem 8.2(a): market up to $6,000
problems.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
problems.prompt: Same both-unperformed $5,000 purchase of truckload of gizmos as 8.1(c). At petition market price for identical goods $6,000. Should trustee assume or reject? Analyze estate net benefit. No answer.

problems.title: Problem 8.2(b): market $4,000, 10% dividend
problems.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
problems.prompt: Same $5,000 contract, market now $4,000; unsecured creditors expected to recover 10% of claims. Should trustee assume or reject, considering estate and rejection damages? No answer.

problems.title: Problem 8.3: profitable but alternate deal and supplier hardship
problems.source: User-uploaded Chapter 8 §§C–D.2 (Trustee options and rejection), full In re Enron Corp. case, original Problems 8.2 and 8.3
problems.prompt: Original both-unperformed $5,000 gizmos contract; market $4,000 but debtor has resale for $5,500 so original contract still yields benefit; unsecured claims paid 50 cents/$1; Jones submits evidence rejection may drive Jones itself bankrupt. Should court approve rejection under competing business-judgment, burden and nondebtor-harm standards? No answer.
